title: Explain transactions with and without Spring Boot (declarative @Transactional vs manual JDBC commit/rollback).
shortTitle: Transactions with and without Spring Boot?

s1_definition.profdef: Without Spring: you manually get a `Connection`, call `setAutoCommit(false)`, execute SQL, call `commit()` on success or `rollback()` on failure, and close the connection in a `finally` block. Error-prone: missing rollback, unclosed connections, no connection pooling. With Spring Boot: `@Transactional` does ALL of this via AOP proxy — one annotation replaces 15+ lines of boilerplate. Spring also adds: connection pooling (HikariCP), retry, timeout, propagation, isolation, and read-replica routing. The proxy IS the 15 lines of manual code, executed reliably every time.
s1_definition.analogy: Without Spring: the teller manually opens the vault, does the work, manually closes the vault, and if they forget to close it on error — the vault stays open all night (connection leak). With Spring: an automatic vault door that opens, lets the teller work, and always closes — even on errors.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Without Spring: you manually get a `Connection`, call `setAutoCommit(false)`, execute SQL, call `commit()` on success or `rollback()` on failure, and close the connection in a `finally` block. Error-prone: missing rollback, unclosed connections, no connection pooling. With Spring Boot: `@Transactional` does ALL of this via AOP proxy — one annotation replaces 15+ lines of boilerplate. Spring also adds: connection pooling (HikariCP), retry, timeout, propagation, isolation, and read-replica routing. The proxy IS the 15 lines of manual code, executed reliably every time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Without Spring: the teller manually opens the vault, does the work, manually closes the vault, and if they forget to close it on error — the vault stays open all night (connection leak). With Spring: an automatic vault door that opens, lets the teller work, and always closes — even on errors.

**One line to remember:** Manual JDBC: get connection, setAutoCommit(false), try-commit-catch-rollback-finally-close. Spring @Transactional: one annotation replaces all of it. Never go manual in production.

sections.s2_technical:
Without Spring, a transaction is entirely manual. You obtain a `Connection`, call `connection.setAutoCommit(false)` to begin, run your SQL, and then `connection.commit()` on success. On any exception you must `connection.rollback()` in a catch block, and in a finally block you must restore auto-commit and close the connection. This is more than fifteen lines of fragile boilerplate with several ways to go wrong: forgetting the rollback leaves partial data, and forgetting to close leaks the connection until the pool is exhausted and the application crashes.

With Spring Boot, `@Transactional` collapses all of that into one annotation. The AOP proxy performs exactly the same steps — get a pooled connection, disable auto-commit, run the method, commit on normal return, roll back on a RuntimeException, and always release the connection — but it does them reliably every single time. On top of that it adds connection pooling via HikariCP, plus configurable propagation, isolation, timeout, read-only routing, and rollbackFor. For example, `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class, timeout = 10)` replaces the entire manual try-commit-catch-rollback-finally-close block and also binds the connection to the thread so multiple repository calls share it. A senior nuance: the proxy is literally the manual code generated for you, which is why production systems always use declarative transactions rather than hand-written JDBC.
sections.s3_banking: **Problem — A legacy banking module uses raw JDBC for fund transfers.** Developers occasionally forget to rollback on error or close connections in finally. Connection leaks exhaust the pool and crash the application. The team migrates to Spring @Transactional.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Rs.50,000 RTGS transfer from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), run once through the manual JDBC path and once through the Spring path.

**Step 1.** In the manual path, the code calls `dataSource.getConnection()`, then `connection.setAutoCommit(false)` to begin. Any slip here — forgetting to disable auto-commit — would make each statement commit on its own.

**Step 2.** It runs the debit UPDATE on SAV2001 and the credit UPDATE on CUR3001 using prepared statements on that same connection, then calls `connection.commit()`. If an exception occurs, the catch block must call `connection.rollback()`, and the finally block must restore auto-commit and close the connection or the connection leaks.

**Step 3.** In the Spring path, the proxy around the service performs the identical sequence automatically: it gets a pooled connection, disables auto-commit, and binds the connection to the thread.

**Step 4.** The real method debits SAV2001 and credits CUR3001 through repositories that share the thread-bound connection. On normal return the proxy commits; on a RuntimeException it rolls back.

**Step 5.** The proxy always releases the connection back to HikariCP, even on error, so there is no leak. Both paths leave SAV2001 at 950,000 and CUR3001 at 300,000, but the Spring path did it with one annotation instead of forty fragile lines.

```
INFO  [exec-1] ManualJdbcTransferService - getConnection, setAutoCommit(false), debit, credit, commit, close
INFO  [exec-1] SpringTransferService - @Transactional proxy: begin, debit, credit, COMMIT, connection released
INFO  [exec-1] SpringTransferService - SAV2001=950000, CUR3001=300000 (no leak)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ WITHOUT SPRING (Manual JDBC) — 40 lines ═══

  transferManual(from, to, amount):
    1. connection = dataSource.getConnection()     ← from HikariCP
    2. connection.setAutoCommit(false)              ← BEGIN TX
    3. PreparedStatement: UPDATE balance - amount WHERE account_id = from
    4. PreparedStatement: UPDATE balance + amount WHERE account_id = to
    5. connection.commit()                          ← COMMIT
    CATCH: connection.rollback()                    ← easy to FORGET!
    FINALLY: connection.close()                     ← LEAK if missed!

    RISKS:
    (Avoid) Forget rollback → partial data (debited but not credited)
    (Avoid) Forget close → connection LEAK → pool exhausted → app CRASHES
    (Avoid) Forget setAutoCommit(false) → each statement auto-commits → no atomicity
    (Avoid) No propagation/isolation/timeout/readOnly support
    (Avoid) Exception in catch/finally → original exception lost

  ═══ WITH SPRING (@Transactional) — 1 annotation ═══

  @Transactional
  transfer(from, to, amount):
    PROXY handles:
    1. getConnection()              (Recommended) automatic
    2. setAutoCommit(false)         (Recommended) automatic
    3. Call real method             (Recommended) your code
    4a. commit() on success         (Recommended) automatic
    4b. rollback() on exception     (Recommended) automatic (RuntimeException)
    5. close() ALWAYS               (Recommended) automatic (even on error)

    PLUS:
    (Recommended) propagation (REQUIRED, REQUIRES_NEW, etc.)
    (Recommended) isolation (READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, etc.)
    (Recommended) timeout (fail if TX exceeds N seconds)
    (Recommended) readOnly (skip dirty checking, route to replica)
    (Recommended) rollbackFor (customize which exceptions rollback)
    (Recommended) Connection bound to thread (multiple repo calls share ONE connection)
```

```
  Manual: getConnection → setAutoCommit(false) → SQL → commit
          catch → rollback ; finally → setAutoCommit(true) → close
  Spring: proxy does ALL of the above automatically + pooling + propagation

  1. Controller.transferSpring(from,to,amt)

  3.     → SpringTransferService.transfer()  debit + credit via repos
  4.   → proxy COMMIT, unbind, close (always, even on error)

  Contract for transfer():
    Pre:  accounts exist, sender has funds
    Post: atomic debit+credit; connection always released (no leak)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Without Spring, transaction management requires manually getting a connection, disabling auto-commit, executing SQL, committing on success, rolling back on failure in the catch block, and closing the connection in a finally block. This is 40 plus lines of boilerplate that is error-prone: forgetting to rollback leaves partial data, forgetting to close leaks the connection and eventually crashes the application. Spring's Transactional annotation replaces all of this with one line. The AOP proxy does exactly what the manual code does but reliably every time, plus it adds propagation, isolation, timeout, readOnly, and rollbackFor configuration that manual JDBC cannot express.

In my RTGS transfer service, both the manual JDBC version and the Spring Transactional version produce the same result: atomic debit and credit. But the manual version has 40 lines of try-catch-finally boilerplate with multiple failure points, while the Spring version is a clean 15-line method with one annotation. The Spring version also automatically binds the connection to the current thread so multiple repository calls share the same connection and participate in the same transaction. In production, we exclusively use declarative Transactional for single operations and TransactionTemplate for batch processing where per-chunk commits are needed.
